summary:
**Project Title:** Unified Active Fire Monitoring & Burning Activity Calendar

Our project explores how NASA satellite observations and machine learning can help us better understand historical wildfire activity and identify locations that may experience future satellite-detected fire activity.

Using historical MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations and supplementary Canadian wildfire reports, we developed a processing pipeline for analyzing geographic and temporal fire patterns.

Our key modeling approach considers not only historical fire-detection counts but also the **time since a location's last recorded detection**. After initially considering linear regression, we selected Random Forest to capture more complex relationships in the data.

Our H3-based model achieved 89.12% classification accuracy on a 2025 holdout dataset and generated experimental detection-probability estimates for 67,766 geographic cells across forecast end years 2026–2035.

These predictions can be explored through a geographic map, helping users examine areas with different historical activity patterns. Our long-term goal is to support better-informed wildfire monitoring and preparedness. Faster access to useful information may help responders make timelier decisions.

The model's forecasts are experimental satellite-detection estimates, not validated operational wildfire warnings. Full MODIS/VIIRS harmonization and a unified burning activity calendar remain development priorities.
details:
Our project, Unified Active Fire Monitoring & Burning Activity Calendar, aims to make historical satellite fire data easier to understand, analyze, and use for forecasting potential fire activity.

The Problem

Wildfires are a significant challenge in Canada, particularly in British Columbia, where they threaten communities, infrastructure, and ecosystems. Faster access to meaningful fire information can support better preparation and more timely responses from firefighters.

NASA provides extensive historical fire-detection data through MODIS and VIIRS satellites. However, these instruments have different resolutions, observation periods, and sensitivities, making their records difficult to compare directly.

Our Solution

We developed a data-processing and machine-learning pipeline that analyzes historical satellite fire detections and generates geographic predictions.

Our project uses NASA MODIS and VIIRS observations alongside supplementary wildfire incident reports from the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre (CIFFC).

We clean and organize historical records, analyze fire-detection patterns, and use machine learning to estimate where future satellite fire activity may be detected.

Our main innovation is incorporating the time since a location's last recorded fire detection as an important model input. Rather than relying only on previous detection counts and geographic coordinates, our model also considers how recently fire activity was observed in each location.

Machine Learning Approach

We initially considered Linear Regression but selected Random Forest because historical fire-detection patterns involve complex, nonlinear relationships.

Our model considers geographic location, previous years of fire detections, historical detection frequency, active detection days, and time since the last recorded detection.

Our latest model, Random Forest V5, achieved 89.12% classification accuracy on a 2025 historical test dataset.

Using H3 hexagonal geographic indexing, we generated predictions for 67,766 geographic cells, with forecast end years ranging from 2026 to 2035.

The resulting 677,660 prediction records are stored in compressed Parquet files, allowing the map to access precomputed results without retraining the model during user interaction.

Technology and Tools

We used Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Random Forest, H3 geospatial indexing, Apache Parquet, PyArrow, Joblib, Docker, Jupyter, GitLab, and interactive visualization tools.

Our approach connects satellite observations, historical feature engineering, machine learning, and geographic visualization.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to help researchers, emergency managers, and firefighters understand historical burning patterns and identify locations that may require closer monitoring.

By making complex satellite information more accessible, the platform could support better-informed wildfire preparedness and, as the system develops, more timely decisions.

Future Improvements

We plan to complete MODIS/VIIRS sensor harmonization, develop the unified burning activity calendar, introduce additional machine learning algorithms, improve model tuning and validation, incorporate weather-related features, and transition the interactive dashboard from Marimo to Dash.

Our current outputs are experimental estimates of satellite fire-detection likelihood, not operational wildfire warnings or validated predictions of when a wildfire will start.
